newsitem.title: USA: Domestic automakers sound alarm over emission restrictions.
newsitem.headline: Domestic automakers sound alarm over emission restrictions.

text.p: If an international treaty restricting carbon dioxide emissions is allowed to go forward it will have a grave affect on the United States and other industrialised countries, top executives from Ford Motor Co. and Chrysler Corp. warned on Wednesday.

Ford Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Alex Trotman said during a speech the proposed treaty on global warming that will be discussed in December in Kyoto, Japan, could lead to higher energy and vehicle prices, and hurt economic output from developed countries.

"It's about the sharing of wealth and jobs for the next 30 years. It's a far bigger issue than what comes out of an automobile's tail pipe," Trotman said at the University of Michigan's annual automotive conference here.

At the meeting during the first week of December, the 152 participating countries in the Conference of Parties to the Framework Convention on Climatic Change will meet for final negotiations and a signing ceremony.

The treaty, which includes the United States, is aimed at curbing emissions that have been found to contribute to global warming. Trotman said the treaty could mean that carbon dioxide emissions in the United States by 2010 would have to be rolled back to 1990 levels, a decrease of 35 percent. That could hurt economic growth, he said, because energy generation is tied directly to increases in the gross domestic product.

A spokesman for the Sierra Club said domestic automakers are ignoring the views of 2,500 climate scientists from around the world who determined that global warming is a real issue caused in large part by pollution from cars and power plants.

"This is yet another case where the auto industry is trying to elevate their short-sighted, short-term profit mentality above the public interest," said Dan Becker, director of the Sierra Club's global warming and energy programme.

However, Tom Gale, executive vice president for product development at Chrysler, said a majority of the 2,000 scientists were in fact social scientists, not experts in atmospheric physics. Gale suggested that the global warming issue should be dealt with using a government-industry partnership approach.

While U.S. automakers complained about the global warming issue, Takeo Fukui, president and chief executive officer of Honda of America Manufacturing, told attendees at the University of Michigan conference that automakers are obligated to produce cleaner cars that people want to buy.

Also on Wednesday, American Honda Motor Co., another unit of Honda Motor Co. Ltd., said it will add 200,000 1998 Civic cars to the low emission vehicles it plans to sell in the United States. The company announced last month it will offer 240,000 1998 Accord sedans with low-emission engines, making it the first automaker to offer low-emission vehicles on a national basis.
